\chapter{Starting and stopping work}
\label{ch:ar-starting-and-stopping-work}
\hlchaptermodality{522}

\begin{chapteropening}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\ar{باشر} (bāshara)}{باشر (bāshara)}]{\ar{باشر} (bāshara) — to set to work, to start on}

\label{lesson:AR-C522-bashara}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Arabic for to promote, then the Arabic for to get tired.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ar{باشر}}
\textbf{\ar{باشر}} — \emph{bāshara} — \textquotedblleft{}to set to work, to start on\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
\ar{باشر} \ar{الموظف} \ar{الجديد} \ar{عمله} \ar{يوم} \ar{الأحد}.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{bāshara al-muwaẓẓaf al-jadīd ʿamalahu yawm al-aḥad.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
The new employee started work on Sunday.
\end{quote}

Present: \ar{يباشر}, \emph{yubāshir}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ar{باشر}} (\emph{bāshara}) is built on the native Arabic root \emph{b-sh-r}, \textquotedblleft{}the skin; to touch directly\textquotedblright{} (Lane). Form III bāshara is to put one's own hand to a task. Mubāshir, direct, which you know, is its participle.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for describing what you lived and felt.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{bāshara}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{bāshara}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{bāshara al-muwaẓẓaf al-jadīd ʿamalahu yawm al-aḥad.} — The new employee started work on Sunday.
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Arabic for to promote, then the Arabic for to get tired, then say \emph{bāshara} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ar{باشر} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}To set to work, to start on\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\texorpdfstring{\ar{كدح} (kadaḥa)}{كدح (kadaḥa)}]{\ar{كدح} (kadaḥa) — to toil}

\label{lesson:AR-C522-kadaha}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Arabic for to get tired, then the Arabic for to set to work.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ar{كدح}}
\textbf{\ar{كدح}} — \emph{kadaḥa} — \textquotedblleft{}to toil\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
\ar{كدح} \ar{المزارع} \ar{في} \ar{الحقل} \ar{طوال} \ar{اليوم}.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{kadaḥa al-muzāriʿ fī al-ḥaql ṭūla al-yawm.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
The farmer toiled in the field all day.
\end{quote}

Present: \ar{يكدح}, \emph{yakdaḥ}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ar{كدح}} (\emph{kadaḥa}) is built on the native Arabic root \emph{k-d-ḥ}, \textquotedblleft{}to labour, to strive\textquotedblright{} (Lane). Lane gives yakdaḥu as its present.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for describing what you lived and felt.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}

\raggedright

  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{kadaḥa}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{kadaḥa al-muzāriʿ fī al-ḥaql ṭūla al-yawm.} — The farmer toiled in the field all day.
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Arabic for to get tired, then the Arabic for to set to work, then say \emph{kadaḥa} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]

\section[\texorpdfstring{\ar{استقالة} (istiqāla)}{استقالة (istiqāla)}]{\ar{استقالة} (istiqāla) — a resignation}

\label{lesson:AR-C522-istiqala}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Arabic for to set to work, then the Arabic for to toil.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ar{استقالة}}
\textbf{\ar{استقالة}} — \emph{istiqāla} — \textquotedblleft{}a resignation\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
\ar{كتب} \ar{الموظف} \ar{استقالته} \ar{وأعطاها} \ar{للمدير}.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{kataba al-muwaẓẓaf istiqālatahu wa-aʿṭāhā li-l-mudīr.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
The employee wrote his resignation and gave it to the manager.
\end{quote}

The verb \ar{استقال}, to resign, goes with it.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ar{استقالة}} (\emph{istiqāla}) is built on the native Arabic root \emph{q-y-l}, \textquotedblleft{}to release from a bargain\textquotedblright{} (Lane). Istiqāla is asking to be released.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for describing what you lived and felt.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{istiqāla}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{istiqāla}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{kataba al-muwaẓẓaf istiqālatahu wa-aʿṭāhā li-l-mudīr.} — The employee wrote his resignation and gave it to the manager.
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Arabic for to set to work, then the Arabic for to toil, then say \emph{istiqāla} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ar{استقالة} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}A resignation\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\texorpdfstring{\ar{متقاعد} (mutaqāʿid)}{متقاعد (mutaqāʿid)}]{\ar{متقاعد} (mutaqāʿid) — retired; a pensioner}

\label{lesson:AR-C522-mutaqaid}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Arabic for to toil, then the Arabic for a resignation.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ar{متقاعد}}
\textbf{\ar{متقاعد}} — \emph{mutaqāʿid} — \textquotedblleft{}retired; a pensioner\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
\ar{جارنا} \ar{معلم} \ar{متقاعد}.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{jārunā muʿallim mutaqāʿid.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
Our neighbour is a retired teacher.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ar{متقاعد}} (\emph{mutaqāʿid}) is built on the native Arabic root \emph{q-ʿ-d}, \textquotedblleft{}to sit\textquotedblright{} (Lane). Mutaqāʿid is the participle of Form VI.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for describing what you lived and felt.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright

  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{mutaqāʿid}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{jārunā muʿallim mutaqāʿid.} — Our neighbour is a retired teacher.
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Arabic for to toil, then the Arabic for a resignation, then say \emph{mutaqāʿid} again
\end{itemize}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\ar{عاطل} (ʿāṭil)}{عاطل (ʿāṭil)}]{\ar{عاطل} (ʿāṭil) — unemployed, out of work}

\label{lesson:AR-C522-atil}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Arabic for a resignation, then the Arabic for retired.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ar{عاطل}}
\textbf{\ar{عاطل}} — \emph{ʿāṭil} — \textquotedblleft{}unemployed, out of work\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
\ar{ابن} \ar{عمي} \ar{عاطل} \ar{عن} \ar{العمل}.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{ibn ʿammī ʿāṭil ʿan al-ʿamal.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
My cousin is out of work.
\end{quote}

The full phrase is \ar{عاطل} \ar{عن} \ar{العمل}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ar{عاطل}} (\emph{ʿāṭil}) is built on the native Arabic root \emph{ʿ-ṭ-l}, \textquotedblleft{}to be empty, without use\textquotedblright{} (Lane). Muʿaṭṭal, out of order, which you know, is from the same root.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for describing what you lived and felt.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{ʿāṭil}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{ʿāṭil}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{ibn ʿammī ʿāṭil ʿan al-ʿamal.} — My cousin is out of work.
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Arabic for a resignation, then the Arabic for retired, then say \emph{ʿāṭil} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ar{عاطل} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}Unemployed, out of work\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
